Chapter 24
Why The Princes Of Italy Have Lost Their States

If a new prince carefully follows the advice I have laid out, he will seem well-established. He will instantly become more secure and firmly rooted in his state than if he had ruled there for generations. The actions of a new prince are watched much more closely than those of a hereditary ruler. When those actions show clear ability, they win over more men and build far stronger loyalty than ancient bloodlines ever could. Men are always drawn more to the present than to the past. When they find the present conditions good, they enjoy them and look no further. In fact, they will fiercely defend a new prince, as long as he does not fail them in other ways. Thus, a new prince will win double the glory: first for creating a new principality, and second for strengthening it with good laws, strong armies, reliable allies, and an excellent example. On the other hand, it is a double disgrace for a man born as a prince to lose his state because of his own incompetence.

Look at the rulers who have lost their states in Italy in our time, such as the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and others. You will find they all shared one common flaw regarding their military forces, for all the reasons I have already explained at length. Furthermore, you will see that some of them either made an enemy of the people, or, if the people were friendly, they failed to secure the loyalty of the nobles. As long as a ruler avoids these specific mistakes, he will not lose a state that has enough power to put an army in the field.

Consider Philip of Macedon. This is not the father of Alexander the Great, but the Philip who was defeated by Titus Quintius. He had very little territory compared to the massive power of Rome and Greece that attacked him. Yet, because he was a warlike man who knew how to win over the people and secure the loyalty of his nobles, he managed to fight off his enemies for many years. Even though he eventually lost control of a few cities, he still held onto his kingdom.

Therefore, our Italian princes should not blame Fortuna for the loss of their states after holding them for so many years. They should blame their own laziness. During times of peace, they never imagined that things could change. It is a common human flaw to fail to prepare for a storm while the weather is calm. When bad times finally arrived, these princes thought only of running away instead of defending themselves. They foolishly hoped that the people, disgusted by the arrogance of the conquerors, would invite them back. This strategy might be acceptable if all other options have failed, but it is a terrible mistake to neglect every other solution just to rely on that one hope. You should never allow yourself to fall simply because you believe someone else will eventually pick you up. Most of the time, that rescue never comes. And even if it does, it will not make you secure, because any deliverance that does not depend on you is completely useless. The only reliable, certain, and lasting defenses are the ones that depend entirely on yourself and your own Virtù.
